title: Robotics from zero
intro_md:
## What is a robot?

> **Key idea:** A robot's useful behavior lives in the closed loop, not in any single sensor or actuator.

- **Robots act on the physical world:** A robot senses its surroundings, computes what to do, and acts on its environment.
- **Robots take many forms:** They include wheeled bases, factory arms, legged machines, and small desktop companions.
- A robot's **control loop** measures, estimates, decides, moves, and measures again.

A webcam provides pixels, a joint encoder provides an angle, and a motor turns an electrical command into torque. A program connects these parts, but the body and environment decide what actions are possible.

A robot differs from a typical web service because its output can move something, contact a person, or fall over. The software must handle uncertain measurements, delays, mechanical limits, and changing surroundings.

- **An SO-101 pick depends on feedback:** The arm locates the cube, translates its position into joint angles, moves its servos, and checks the result.
- **A command does not confirm a grasp:** Check whether the gripper actually picked up the object.

![SO-101 leader arm used to teleoperate a follower robot](/img/lessons/guide-intro-robot-loop.webp)
*SO-101 leader arm used to teleoperate a follower robot. Source: [LeRobot SO-101 documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/so101), license unknown.*

## The fields of robotics and how they fit together

Robotics combines several fields into one working system:

- **Mechanisms and actuation** define the links, joints, wheels, and motors.
- **Embedded electronics** connect computers to sensors and actuators.
- **Sensing and perception** measure the world and turn camera pixels into objects or marker poses.
- **Kinematics and dynamics** relate joint angles to tool position and describe forces and motion.
- **Control and planning** choose motor commands and routes or arm trajectories that avoid obstacles.
- **State estimation and SLAM** combine noisy measurements to estimate position while building a map.
- **Simulation and robot learning** test a model before hardware and use demonstrations or interaction data to train policies.
- **Human–robot interaction (HRI)** studies how people understand and safely work with robots.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S["Sense: camera, encoder"] --> E["Estimate: pose, velocity"]
  E --> P["Plan: next motion"]
  P --> A["Act: motors move"]
  A --> S
```

## Hardware vs software: what changes when code touches the real world

- **Robotics software uses familiar tools:** It relies on functions, data structures, tests, logs, and version control.
- **Hardware adds noisy, delayed inputs and outputs:** Physical devices connect software to the changing world.
- **Hardware adds delays and limits:** Motors may move slowly under load, cameras may return blurry frames, wheels may slip, and commands may saturate.
- **Simulation cannot guarantee hardware success:** A program that works in a small simulation can fail on the real robot.

Use the same habits you use when debugging a distributed system: timestamp measurements, record versions, make failures observable, and test one component at a time. Add robotics-specific checks too: units, coordinate frames, joint limits, power, and physical clearance.

- **Unlabeled units invite mistakes:** A target of 0.3 may mean meters, centimeters, or a normalized value; label units at system boundaries.
- **Missing sensors need explicit errors:** A controller should report a missing sensor instead of silently treating its reading as zero.

## How to use these maps

- **The world map** helps you find organizations, robots, projects, and their connections. The Holygraph whiteboard arranges knowledge and projects by branch and learning level, showing prerequisites.
- Start with an interesting **node**, read its summary, then open its lesson and resources.
- **Suggested paths are not exams:** Skip prerequisites you already understand when following a “start here” route.
- **Groups** collect a team's project stack; Guide chat can clarify questions when available.

- Prefer current **official documentation or papers** for exact commands and specifications.
- **Blog posts and videos** are useful for seeing a system move; they may show an older software version.
- Record the **device model**, firmware, library version, and measurement units before reproducing an example.

- **Map scope:** It describes relationships, not guaranteed compatibility or support.

## Suggested order

- Start by learning **physical vocabulary**, then build skills in this order.

1. **Learn the body:** links, joints, actuators, voltage, sensors, and coordinate frames.
2. **Control in simulation:** write a small controller and inspect its response.
3. **Measure a target:** use a camera or marker to estimate where an object is.
4. **Plan and estimate:** learn how planning converts a target into motion and how calibration and state estimation handle uncertainty.
5. **Learn from data:** collect demonstrations or train a robot policy.
6. **Try a practical chain:** assemble a SO-101, teleoperate it, record several safe demonstrations, train or run a baseline policy, then evaluate on new object positions.

chapters.title: Mechanisms & actuation: giving a robot a body
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** The actuator sets available force, but the linkage decides where that force can move.

- **Mechanical structure and actuation:** Links, joints, wheels, gears, belts, and grippers constrain movement; an actuator supplies motion.
- **A LeRobot SO-101 arm** makes this visible: six joints move a wrist-mounted gripper, and the follower uses six FEETECH STS3215 servos.

Changing link length changes reach and leverage before a line of software is written.

![FEETECH STS3215 serial bus servo actuator](/img/lessons/guide-mechanisms-actuation.webp)
*FEETECH STS3215 serial bus servo actuator. Source: [FEETECH STS3215 product page](https://www.feetech.cn/en/74v-19-kgcm-plastic-case-metal-tooth-magnetic-code-double-axis-ttl-series-steering-gear.html), license unknown.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop

- **Mechanisms form the physical output stage:** A command becomes motor torque; gears and links turn it into movement, and encoders report joint position.
- **Long arms increase shoulder load:** They reach farther but magnify the load; wheel slip also breaks the assumption that motor rotation equals distance traveled.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  L["Links and joints"] --> M["Motor and gearbox"]
  M --> T["Torque at the tool"]
  T --> S["Sensor feedback"]
```

## The big ideas

- **Links and joints define motion:** A link is a relatively rigid segment; a joint lets two links move relative to each other. The SO-101 shoulder is one example.
- **A 1:345 gear ratio trades speed for torque:** The motor turns 345 times per output turn; friction and backlash make real gears less ideal.
- **Workspace depends on geometry:** Longer reach raises shoulder torque demand, and joint placement may block reaching behind the base.
- **Torque and backlash constrain movement:** Torque is turning effort; backlash is lost motion when teeth switch contact after reversal. A mechanism exposes only motions its structure permits.

## What you'll be able to build

- Sketch a **two-link arm**, mark its joints, identify its motor and gripper, and predict which link sees the largest load.
- **The SO-101 and ANYmal solve different tasks:** Compare the arm's compact tabletop reach with ANYmal's four-legged structure.
- Begin with **actuator sizing** and gear trains, then model a part in CAD.
- **Check clearance before powering hardware:** Keep the arm from hitting a table or person throughout its range.

chapters.title: Embedded & electronics: connecting code to hardware
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** Timing and electrical limits are part of a robot's behavior, not implementation details.

Embedded electronics are the circuits and small computers that let software communicate with motors and sensors. A microcontroller reads a command, updates an output pin or bus, and repeats on a fixed schedule.

On the SO-101, a host computer talks to FEETECH servos through a serial bus; the motor's control board handles the low-level position loop while LeRobot coordinates the arm.

![Labelled ESP32-DevKitC board showing ports and components](/img/lessons/guide-embedded-electronics.webp)
*Labelled ESP32-DevKitC board showing ports and components. Source: [Espressif ESP32-DevKitC guide](https://documentation.espressif.com/esp-dev-kits/en/latest/esp32/esp32-devkitc/user_guide.html), license unknown.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop

- **Electronic path:** Program commands pass through a processor and interface to actuators; sensors return feedback. **UART** sends serial bits; **I²C** uses a clocked two-wire bus.
- **SPI exchanges peripheral data:** It uses clock and data lines for faster exchange; **CAN** is a robust multi-node bus used in many mobile robots.
- **Bus choice depends on requirements:** Consider distance, speed, wiring, and fault tolerance.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C["Robot program"] --> B["Embedded board"]
  B --> G["GPIO or serial"]
  G --> D["Device signal"]
  D --> B
```

## The big ideas

- **Voltage and current describe electricity:** Voltage is potential difference, current is charge flow, and power is their product; logic pins encode 0 or 1 but cannot power a motor.
- **The SO-101 servos share a serial bus:** Each of six follower servos has an ID, so a command to joint 3 needs no separate USB cable.
- **UART, I²C, SPI, and CAN differ:** UART sends serial bits; I²C is a clocked two-wire bus; SPI uses clock/data for faster peripherals; CAN is a robust multi-node bus.
- **A watchdog responds to missing heartbeats:** It can put an actuator into a defined state; treat addresses, packets, timing, and error replies like a network protocol.

## What you'll be able to build

- Trace a **sensor wire** to its processor and explain where motor power enters the circuit.
- Follow the **LeRobot wiring and setup instructions**, then check a servo's voltage and protocol limits before connecting it.
- **Verify a servo reply:** Send a position request to one servo ID and confirm the reply reports the expected ID and position.
- **Check basic communication faults:** Silence suggests a power, wiring, baud-rate, or ID mismatch.

chapters.title: Sensing: measuring the world
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** A measurement is useful only when its units, timing, and uncertainty are understood.

Sensing turns physical events into numbers a program can use. An encoder reports shaft rotation, an inertial measurement unit (IMU) reports acceleration and angular rate, and a camera reports pixels.

The SO-101's joint servos include magnetic encoders, so LeRobot can observe joint positions; a separate webcam can show whether the gripper is over a target.

![OpenCV camera image showing an ArUco marker sheet before detection](/img/lessons/project-webcam-apriltags.webp)
*OpenCV camera image showing an ArUco marker sheet before detection. Source: [OpenCV ArUco detection tutorial](https://docs.opencv.org/4.13.0/d5/dae/tutorial_aruco_detection.html), license unknown.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop

- **Sensors close the loop:** A command changes the robot; sensors measure the result, and software updates its next action. Measurements are not the world itself.
- **Sensors report different quantities:** A camera records a 2-D projection; an IMU measures motion plus bias and vibration; an encoder measures angle but cannot detect wheel slip.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W["World signal"] --> S["Sensor reading"]
  S --> C["Calibration"]
  C --> E["Task estimate"]
```

## The big ideas

- **Resolution, noise, and bias differ:** Resolution is the smallest detectable change, noise is random variation, and bias is a persistent offset; encoders, IMUs, and cameras answer different questions.
- **Camera intrinsics model the lens:** Focal length and optical center describe projection; distortion coefficients model lens bending, and checkerboard images support calibration.
- **A known 0.10 m AprilTag provides scale:** Its physical corner spacing converts image pixels into meters during pose estimation.
- **Sensor output is uncertain:** Like an API response, a measurement is evidence rather than perfect ground truth.

## What you'll be able to build

- **Compare sensors by direct evidence:** Ask what encoder, IMU, and camera data directly measure versus what each only implies.
- Photograph a checkerboard from several angles during **webcam calibration**, estimate the camera matrix, then use it before estimating tag pose.
- **OpenCV's current ArUco tutorial** demonstrates detection and pose estimation; AprilTag and ArUco families and APIs are not interchangeable.
- Record a **sensor value** with its timestamp and units before using it in a robot loop.

chapters.title: Kinematics & dynamics: describing robot motion
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** A transform chain, not a raw joint value, tells where the tool sits in the world.

Kinematics describes motion without asking what forces caused it; dynamics studies the forces and masses that do. A robot arm is a chain of coordinate frames attached to its base, links, and tool.

If a camera sees a tag 0.30 m in front of it and the camera is mounted 0.10 m above the arm base, transforming between those frames lets the robot express the tag location relative to its gripper.

![Robot links annotated with Denavit-Hartenberg frames and parameters](/img/lessons/guide-kinematics-dynamics.webp)
*Robot links annotated with Denavit-Hartenberg frames and parameters. Source: [Wikimedia Commons Denavit-Hartenberg diagram](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Denavit-Hartenberg-Transformations_Robot.svg), Public domain.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop

- **Planning specifies a tool target:** A motion planner may request that the tool move to a point in the room.
- **Motors need joint angles:** Forward kinematics maps joint angles to tool pose; inverse kinematics searches for angles that produce a requested pose.
- **Dynamics predicts required torque:** It describes what links need while accelerating or holding a load.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  J["Joint angles"] --> F["Forward kinematics"]
  F --> P["Tool pose"]
  P --> I["Inverse kinematics"]
  I --> J
```

## The big ideas

- **A coordinate frame has an origin and axes:** A homogeneous transform is a 4×4 matrix combining rotation and translation.
- **Forward and inverse kinematics solve different directions:** Forward maps joint values to tool pose; inverse finds joint values for a target pose.
- **Frame B sits 2 m right of A with a counter-clockwise rotation:** The 90° rotation maps point B=(1,0,0) to (0,1,0).
- **Translation then gives A=(2,1,0):** Reversing rotation and translation produces a different result.
- **ROS 2 `tf2` stores timestamped transforms:** Frame labels act like software types; adding a camera-frame point directly to a map-frame point is a coordinate bug.

## What you'll be able to build

- Draw the **base, shoulder, elbow, and tool frames** on an SO-101, then explain how a target point moves through the chain.
- Apply a **4×4 transform** by hand and label both the source and destination frames.
- Begin with **rigid-body transforms** before forward kinematics; this avoids treating a measured joint angle as a world-space position.

chapters.title: Control: making motors do what you mean
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** A controller must act on measured error and respect what the plant can deliver.

Control makes a robot follow a target despite disturbances and imperfect models. A motor controller compares desired position with measured position and changes motor effort to reduce the error.

On a SO-101 joint, if the target is 30° and the encoder reads 24°, the error is +6°; the controller must move the joint toward the target without overshooting or oscillating.

![PID feedback-control diagram showing plant, controller, and measured output](/img/lessons/knowledge-pid.webp)
*PID feedback-control diagram showing plant, controller, and measured output. Source: [Wikimedia Commons PID feedback diagram](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PID_en_updated_feedback.svg), CC BY-SA 3.0.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop

- **Controller loop:** Read sensors, compute error, choose an output, and send it to an actuator.
- **Proportional** reacts to current error, **integral** accumulates persistent error, and **derivative** responds to how quickly error changes; together they form PID control.
- **Gain is a trade-off:** Too much makes the arm shake; too little makes it sluggish.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  R["Reference position"] --> E["Position error"]
  E --> P["PID controller"]
  P --> M["Motor command"]
  M --> S["Measured position"]
  S --> E
```

## The big ideas

- **The sampling period sets update timing:** A controller designed for 10 ms behaves differently if it actually updates every 100 ms.
- **PID combines three responses:** P reacts to current error, I to accumulated error, and D to the error's rate of change.
- **A 10° error with gain 0.4 gives 4 units:** That proportional output is before actuator limits.
- **Saturation caps output at the motor limit:** Integral windup keeps accumulating error while the output is capped.
- **Tune against the physical load:** Mass, gearing, friction, and load matter; the retry-and-correct analogy ends where the controller moves hardware.

## What you'll be able to build

- **Position control starts in simulation:** Implement a tiny position loop before testing a motor.
- **A 0.4 gain produces 0.8 output:** With target 10 and measured value 8, error is 2; the proportional output is before limits.
- Add **integral action** only if a constant load leaves a steady error.
- **The MathWorks Tech Talk** visualizes each term; ROS 2 Control documents the controller interface used in real robot stacks.

chapters.title: Simulation: practice in a computed world
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** A simulation is valuable when its assumptions and model mismatch are made explicit.

A robot simulator computes a virtual robot's motion so a team can test ideas before using hardware. A scene contains geometry, mass, joints, contact surfaces, and sensors; a physics engine advances them in small time steps.

MuJoCo is used for research and robotics examples, while NVIDIA Isaac Lab builds GPU-accelerated robot-learning environments on Isaac Sim.

![MuJoCo model-gallery render of the Cassie biped on a simulation grid](/img/lessons/guide-simulation.webp)
*MuJoCo model-gallery render of the Cassie biped on a simulation grid. Source: [MuJoCo model gallery](https://mujoco.readthedocs.io/en/stable/models.html), license unknown.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop

- **The control loop is shared:** In simulation and on hardware, a policy or controller reads sensors, produces actions, and receives the next state.
- **Simulation is only a model:** A frictionless simulation may let a gripper succeed even when the same smooth object slips in reality.
- **Timing, contact, camera exposure**, actuator limits, and noise can create sim-to-real gaps.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M["Robot model"] --> H["Physics step"]
  H --> S["Simulated sensors"]
  S --> C["Controller"]
  C --> H
```

## The big ideas

- **A time step sets update frequency:** A 0.02 s step gives 50 simulated updates per second; 0.01 s gives 100 and costs more computation.
- **Collision shapes approximate solid geometry:** A simple box or capsule can replace a detailed visual mesh for faster contact checks.
- **Validate the model inputs:** Check units, mass, joint limits, and friction.
- **Contact exchanges forces:** Model fidelity describes how closely the simulation assumptions match the real robot.
- **A simulation result is setup-specific:** Passing in MuJoCo or Isaac Lab is evidence about that setup, not proof about the physical SO-101.

## What you'll be able to build

- Start with a **one-joint pendulum** or an arm moving a cube, then compare the same trajectory in MuJoCo and Isaac Lab.
- **The Isaac Lab installation** tutorial shows a real workflow: launch an example task and observe simulated agents learning locomotion.
- **Record the simulator version**, time step, and random seed so another student can reproduce the run. Add sensor noise and imperfect friction before judging whether a learned policy is robust.

chapters.title: Perception: turning sensor data into meaning
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** A detection becomes actionable only after calibration and conversion into the robot's frame.

- **Perception:** Turn sensor measurements into useful descriptions of objects and places.
- **A camera supports marker-pose estimates:** A detector may report “AprilTag ID 7 is 0.6 m ahead, rotated 10°”; calibration, image quality, and marker geometry affect the estimate.

A robot can then align its gripper or estimate its location relative to a known tag.

![OpenCV ArUco marker image after perspective correction](/img/lessons/guide-perception.webp)
*OpenCV ArUco marker image after perspective correction. Source: [OpenCV ArUco detection tutorial](https://docs.opencv.org/4.13.0/d5/dae/tutorial_aruco_detection.html), license unknown.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop

- **Perception connects sensing to decisions:** It interprets raw measurements before planning or control.
- **Perception pipeline:** A camera driver returns pixels; detection finds corners and decodes a marker; pose estimation computes a 3-D transform for planning or control.
- **No detection is not zero:** Distinguish an undetected tag from one at the origin or a valid zero-valued measurement.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I["Camera image"] --> F["Features or tags"]
  F --> O["Object identity"]
  O --> P["Object pose"]
  P --> D["Task decision"]
```

## The big ideas

- **A fiducial marker has a designed identity:** A dictionary is the set of marker codes a detector searches.
- **AprilTag and ArUco are related families:** They use square markers, but their libraries differ.
- **OpenCV 4.13.0 decodes and estimates pose:** Its ArUco pipeline finds candidate squares, decodes an ID, then estimates position and orientation from corners.
- **Each detection stage can fail:** Blur, occlusion, or the wrong dictionary can break the pipeline.
- **Intrinsics and known tag size recover scale:** A 0.10 m edge lets pixel corners estimate metric distance; attach confidence and a coordinate frame.

## What you'll be able to build

- Put a **printed tag** in front of a calibrated webcam and display its ID and corner locations.
- **A known marker supports range estimation:** A calibrated camera and 0.10 m tag can distinguish a small nearby tag from a same-sized distant tag.
- Use the current **OpenCV 4.x API**, not the obsolete 4.0.1 calibration page; record the camera model and tag family.

chapters.title: State estimation & SLAM: knowing where the robot is
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** Combine sensors with complementary errors, and carry uncertainty with the estimate.

State estimation combines imperfect sensor readings into a best estimate of what a robot is doing.

A mobile robot may use wheel encoders for motion, an IMU for rotation, and a camera or GPS for position. **SLAM** means simultaneous localization and mapping: estimate the robot's location while building a map of an unknown environment.

![Hector SLAM video frame showing a laser scan and built map](/img/lessons/guide-state-estimation-slam.webp)
*Hector SLAM video frame showing a laser scan and built map. Source: [Wikimedia Commons Hector SLAM video](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hector_slam_use.webm), CC BY-SA 4.0.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop

- **State estimation prepares sensor data for planning:** An estimator turns noisy measurements into a time-stamped state; wheel odometry drifts as small errors accumulate.
- **Landmarks can correct drift:** A camera may recognize one, and a Kalman filter combines predictions with noisy measurements while tracking uncertainty.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U["Motion input"] --> P["Predict state"]
  P --> M["Measurement update"]
  M --> E["Estimate and uncertainty"]
  E --> L["Map and pose"]
  L --> P
```

## The big ideas

- **The 1-D Kalman state is position:** Predict 10 m with variance 4 m²; GPS measures 12 m with variance 1 m².
- **The Kalman gain is 4/(4+1)=0.8:** The estimate becomes 10+0.8(12−10)=11.6 m and variance becomes 0.8 m².
- **Precise GPS corrects motion prediction:** Wheel odometry, an IMU, and camera landmarks can provide complementary measurements.
- **SLAM estimates location while building a map:** It combines localization and map construction.
- **The newest estimate is not always best:** Like merging timestamped logs with confidence, an estimator needs agreeing clocks and coordinate frames.

## What you'll be able to build

- Plot **predicted and corrected positions** on a line, then add noisy wheel and GPS samples.
- **Inspect how uncertainty shrinks** after a reliable measurement and grows while the robot moves without observations.
- **The ROS `robot_localization` package** applies these ideas to robot messages, while the Python book makes the update equations runnable.
- **Estimates are not ground truth:** The result includes assumptions and uncertainty.

chapters.title: Planning: choosing a route or motion
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** A valid route is a sequence of feasible states, not merely a line toward the goal.

- **Planning:** Choose a sequence of safe motions from a start to a goal.
- **Planning covers routes and arm paths:** A mobile robot may need a corridor route; an arm may need a collision-free joint path to a cup.
- **Geometry and obstacles constrain motion:** The map and robot shape determine which paths are possible.

Planning often returns a path; a controller still has to track it.

![MoveIt motion-planning request, pipeline, and response diagram](/img/lessons/guide-planning.webp)
*MoveIt motion-planning request, pipeline, and response diagram. Source: [MoveIt motion-planning concepts](https://moveit.picknik.ai/main/doc/concepts/motion_planning.html), license unknown.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop

- **The navigation pipeline links three stages:** Perception supplies obstacles and pose; a planner finds a route; a controller sends wheel or joint commands.
- **Nav2** handles mobile navigation in ROS 2, while **MoveIt** plans arm motion.
- **A plan depends on current constraints:** The map, robot footprint, joint limits, and collision model matter; a stale map can invalidate a path.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  G["Goal and map"] --> S["Search states"]
  S --> C["Check collisions"]
  C --> T["Trajectory"]
  T --> R["Robot controller"]
```

## The big ideas

- **Configuration space represents robot poses:** A configuration is a pose or joint-angle vector; each possible configuration is a point, and collisions are forbidden.
- **A* uses cost plus estimated distance:** A* (A-star), a grid search that always expands the cell with the lowest cost-so-far plus estimated distance to the goal, can route around it.
- **A grid detour avoids the blocked cell:** If the direct route from (0,0) to (2,0) hits a wall, pass through (0,1), (1,1), and (2,1).
- **RRT grows a sampled tree:** It grows through sampled configurations, which suits high-dimensional arms.
- **A planner returns a proposed path, not motor commands:** It needs a valid map and constraints; a controller still applies timing and velocity limits.

## What you'll be able to build

- **Create a 2-D grid** with a rectangular obstacle, run A* (A-star), and compare the result with a straight-line route that collides.
- **Then use a simulator** or Nav2 to plan a path for a differential-drive robot. On an arm, inspect MoveIt's collision scene and plan a grasp approach.
- **Start with a small** deterministic map before debugging a full sensor-driven environment.

chapters.title: Manipulation: reaching, grasping, and moving objects
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** Contact changes the task: verify the object's outcome, not only the gripper command.

Manipulation is using a robot arm, hand, or gripper to change the world. Pick-and-place sounds simple—reach, grasp, lift, move, release—but each step depends on geometry, force, contact, and uncertainty.

The SO-101 has a parallel gripper at the end of a six-joint arm; ALOHA uses two low-cost arms to collect demonstrations for bimanual tasks.

![Robot arm reaching toward an object in the MIT manipulation example](/img/lessons/guide-manipulation.webp)
*Robot arm reaching toward an object in the MIT manipulation example. Source: [MIT manipulation pick example](https://manipulation.csail.mit.edu/pick.html), license unknown.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop

- **Manipulation pipeline:** Estimate an object's pose, choose a grasp, plan an approach, close the gripper, verify movement, then plan a transfer.
- **A 2 cm pose error can miss a grasp:** A narrow gripper may miss when its pose estimate is off by 2 cm.
- **Tactile or motor-current feedback** can help detect contact, but a basic setup may use camera images and joint positions only.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  O["Find object"] --> R["Plan a reach"]
  R --> A["Approach and contact"]
  A --> G["Close gripper"]
  G --> V["Verify the grasp"]
```

## The big ideas

- **The SO-101 ends in a parallel gripper:** ALOHA uses two arms for bimanual work; a grasp is a contact arrangement that holds an object.
- **Workspace limits where the tool can reach:** A trajectory is a timed sequence of positions.
- **A 2 cm pose error can miss a narrow gripper:** Plan a clear approach, align, close, check contact, lift, and verify that the object moved.
- **Contact force is exchanged at touching surfaces:** Stable contact balances weight and disturbance.
- **Treat manipulation like a transaction:** Observe, attempt, verify, then commit the transfer—or recover instead of reporting success.

## What you'll be able to build

- Place a **cube** on a table and teleoperate the SO-101 to pick it up.
- Use a **fixed camera** to mark the object's center, and record each attempt so misses can be diagnosed.
- **ACT uses action chunks** for tasks such as bimanual manipulation; LeRobot provides a current recording and rollout workflow.
- **Clear the arm’s path before powered tests:** Use lightweight objects and keep hands out of the mechanism’s travel.

chapters.title: Locomotion: moving through the world
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** Each footfall constrains balance and the body's next motion.

Locomotion is how a robot moves its body through the world. Wheeled bases roll; legged robots alternate contact between feet; tracked robots distribute force over a belt. ETH Zurich's ANYmal is a quadruped designed for rough industrial environments.

Its legs can step over uneven ground where a small differential-drive robot would get stuck.

![ANYmal quadruped walking through a rocky cave environment](/img/lessons/guide-locomotion.webp)
*ANYmal quadruped walking through a rocky cave environment. Source: [ETH RSL ANYmal media page](https://rsl.ethz.ch/robots-media/anymal.html), license unknown.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop

- **Locomotion uses feedback:** Estimate body motion, choose foot placements or wheel speeds, and control joints or motors while the ground pushes back.
- **Gaits alternate contact and swing:** A gait is a repeating pattern of foot contacts and swings.
- **Locomotion sensors reveal different states:** An IMU estimates body orientation, encoders report leg configuration, and contact sensors show whether a step landed.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  V["Desired velocity"] --> G["Gait phase"]
  G --> F["Foot contacts"]
  F --> B["Body balance"]
  B --> S["Sensors update"]
  S --> G
```

## The big ideas

- **Wheels roll and tracks spread force:** Legged robots use a gait, a repeating contact pattern; ETH Zurich's ANYmal is a quadruped for rough terrain.
- **Stance supports the body; swing moves a foot:** Faster motion needs timed placement and center-of-mass control.
- **Dynamic stability maintains balance through motion:** Momentum and foot timing matter.
- **Each foot alternates support and flight:** The controller coordinates these phases using body orientation, joint encoders, and contact feedback.

## What you'll be able to build

- **Plot a gait timeline** for a slow quadruped, showing stance and swing for each leg.
- **Wheels and legs move differently:** A two-wheeled robot turns by setting left and right wheel speeds.
- **ANYmal videos show rough-terrain challenges:** ETH RSL's open `rsl_rl` project demonstrates reinforcement learning for legged policies.
- **Measure gait before judging movement:** In simulation, measure body tilt and foot slip instead of judging by appearance alone.

chapters.title: Robot learning: improving behavior from data
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** A learned policy is only as reliable as its demonstration coverage and evaluation.

- **Robot learning:** Use data and optimization to produce a policy that maps observations to actions.
- **Students collect demonstrations:** Teleoperate an SO-101 to pick up a cube while recording camera images and joint positions.
- **Behavior cloning imitates human actions:** Train on each recorded moment to copy the action selected by the human.

The policy is then tested on new starts, lighting, and object positions.

![Robot-arm task demonstrations shown in the SmolVLA project blog](/img/lessons/guide-robot-learning.webp)
*Robot-arm task demonstrations shown in the SmolVLA project blog. Source: [Hugging Face SmolVLA blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/smolvla), license unknown.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop

- **A learned policy can complement hand-written logic:** LeRobot records synchronized episodes, trains models, and runs rollouts inside the robot loop.
- **ACT predicts short action chunks:** Action Chunking with Transformers predicts sequences rather than single actions.
- **SmolVLA emits continuous action chunks:** This 450-million-parameter vision-language-action model takes camera images, robot state, and a natural-language instruction.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D["Teleoperation demos"] --> E["Episode dataset"]
  E --> T["Train policy"]
  T --> H["Held-out evaluation"]
  H --> R["Robot behavior"]
```

## The big ideas

- **A policy maps observations to actions:** Behavior cloning is supervised learning from demonstrations.
- **An SO-101 demonstration records a cube pick:** Capture camera frames and joint positions while teleoperating, then train on those examples.
- **One start pose may not teach recovery:** Generalization means success in conditions that differ from training, such as a shifted object.
- **Evaluate held-out episodes:** Count task completions and failures, not only training loss or one successful clip.
- **LeRobot synchronizes recorded data:** ACT predicts action chunks; SmolVLA has 450 million parameters.

## What you'll be able to build

- **Evaluate a 50-episode baseline:** Record pick-and-place demonstrations, train a baseline, and test on object positions absent from the demonstrations.
- **The SmolVLA docs recommend** starting with about 50 episodes and give a current `lerobot-train` command; the LeRobot real-world tutorial documents recording and rollout. Compare success rates, not only model loss.
- **Test first in simulation**, then on a slow, supervised, low-payload setup.

chapters.title: HRI & safety: working responsibly around people
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** Predictable behavior and explicit boundaries are the foundation of safe collaboration.

Human–robot interaction (HRI) studies how people and robots share tasks, spaces, and expectations. A robot can be technically correct yet confusing if its intent is invisible.

Pollen Robotics' Reachy Mini is a small expressive desktop robot designed for interaction; an industrial collaborative robot, or cobot, shares a work area with people under specific risk controls.

![Universal Robots UR16e collaborative arm with teach pendant](/img/lessons/guide-hri-safety.webp)
*Universal Robots UR16e collaborative arm with teach pendant. Source: [Wikimedia Commons UR16e robot arm](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:UR16e_robot_arm.png), CC BY-SA 4.0.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop

- **HRI connects sensing, planning, motion, and human feedback.**
- **Human-aware interaction has three stages:** Detect relevant actions, decide whether to move, and communicate through motion, lights, sound, or a screen.
- **Risk assessment identifies hazards:** Ask what can go wrong, who could be harmed, and which safeguards reduce risk before deployment.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I["Task intent"] --> W["Shared workspace"]
  W --> A["Risk assessment"]
  A --> M["Robot motion"]
  M --> O["Monitor people"]
```

## The big ideas

- **HRI includes how robots communicate intent:** Motion, lights, sound, and screens shape interaction.
- **Reachy Mini is expressive; a cobot shares safeguarded space:** A collaborative robot is designed to work near people under safeguards.
- **A hazard can cause harm; risk combines likelihood and severity:** Reach, speed, payload, sharp edges, and unexpected restart affect task risk.
- **A safety-rated stop is a validated system function:** It is not an application-level message.
- **ISO/TS 15066 and machine instructions inform protection:** An interface is like a public API, but a light cannot replace a physical safeguard.

## What you'll be able to build

- Map the arm's **reachable workspace**, identify pinch points, and write a task-specific hazard table before a demo.
- **Risk depends on the platform:** A low-force Reachy Mini and a heavier tool-carrying arm pose different risks at the same distance and speed.
- **Use safety guidance before testing:** Check CCOHS and NIOSH material, then consult manufacturer instructions for the robot’s operating limits.
- Never test a **powered arm** near a person without the lab's approved risk controls.

chapters.title: The robotics world
chapters.body_md:
## What this field is about

> **Key idea:** Robotics advances through shared interfaces, data, hardware, and community feedback.

- **The robotics ecosystem links labs, projects, companies, and communities.**
- A student can assemble a low-cost **SO-101**, record data with Hugging Face LeRobot, explore Pollen Robotics' Reachy, and read ETH Zurich RSL's ANYmal research.

The field is not one product category: it spans tabletop arms, mobile robots, legged machines, and software that connects them.

![Participants at the Hugging Face LeRobot Worldwide Hackathon hosted in 42 Paris](/img/lessons/guide-robotics-world.webp)
*LeRobot Worldwide Hackathon participants at 42 Paris. Source: [42AI LeRobot Hackathon highlights](https://42-ai.github.io/posts/LeRobotHackathonHighlights/), license unknown.*

## Where it sits in the robot loop


- **Organizations contribute different layers:** FEETECH supplies actuators; Hugging Face maintains robot-learning software and datasets; Pollen Robotics develops open humanoid platforms; ETH RSL publishes locomotion research and builds field robots.
- **Research papers, repositories, and product docs serve different roles:** Papers describe methods, repositories expose code, and docs explain device use.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  T["Team needs"] --> L["Lab and robot stack"]
  L --> E["Experiment"]
  E --> R["Results"]
  R --> C["Community knowledge"]
```

## The big ideas

- **An ecosystem connects organizations, tools, products, and communities:** FEETECH supplies actuators; Hugging Face maintains LeRobot tools and datasets.
- **Pollen Robotics builds expressive robots:** Reachy is one example; ETH Zurich RSL researches legged platforms such as ANYmal.
- **Map relations describe links, not rankings:** Built by connects a robot to its maker; Uses connects projects to tools; Prerequisite connects lessons to prior knowledge.
- **Follow one concrete learning chain:** SO-101 hardware → LeRobot teleoperation → recorded demonstrations → ACT or SmolVLA.
- **A demo depends on a supply chain:** Hardware, drivers, data, code, and maintainers connect like software components.

## What you'll be able to build

- **Pick one path through** the map: SO-101 hardware → LeRobot teleoperation → recorded demonstrations → ACT or SmolVLA inference.
- **Robot bodies need different tests:** Compare the SO-101 path with ETH RSL’s ANYmal research; different bodies require different controllers and testing.
- **When approaching a lab** or company, ask a concrete question about a project, dataset, event, or open issue rather than sending a generic request.
- **Start with the linked** papers, documentation, and repositories, then follow their contributors and releases.
